title: Minoan eruption of Thera (Santorini)
summary: The Minoan eruption of Santorini (Thera), Greece, spread ash across the Eastern Mediterranean and buried Bronze Age settlements such as Akrotiri. Its date is debated: radiocarbon dating of a buried olive branch gave 1627–1600 BCE (95%), while archaeologists have traditionally placed it in the mid- to late-16th century BCE. A 2023 recalibration gave late 17th to mid-16th century BCE.

uncertainty.note: Radiocarbon (Friedrich et al. 2006): 1627-1600 BCE (2 sigma) = -1626 to -1599. Archaeological view: mid- to late-16th century BCE; the end of the range (-1500) is an approximation of "late 16th century" for display, not a sourced number. Raj et al. 2023: late 17th to mid-16th century BCE.

as_recorded.value: late 17th century BCE to mid-16th century BCE

when.display: c. 1627–1500 BCE (radiocarbon 1627–1600 BCE; archaeology mid- to late-16th century BCE)

where.historical_name: Thera, Aegean Sea; Minoan-influenced Bronze Age Cyclades

importance.justification: A major Bronze Age eruption whose ash layer is a dating marker for the Eastern Mediterranean, and whose date is a central chronology dispute.

perspectives.account: Olive branch buried in the eruption pumice dated to 1627-1600 BCE at 95% confidence.
Based on Aegean-Egyptian cultural links, placed the eruption in the mid- to late-16th century BCE.
Recalibration with moving-average curves gives a late 17th to mid-16th century BCE span.
